method: A bridge ID is the 2-byte bridge priority followed by the 48-bit MAC address, and the switch with the lowest bridge ID wins the root election, so priority is compared before the MAC and a priority of 4096 beats the default 32768 whatever the MAC is. Each remaining switch selects the port that offers the lowest root path cost, exactly as the root path cost and designated port vectors are compared in IEEE 802.1D: lowest root path cost first, then the lowest upstream bridge ID, then the lowest upstream port ID, then the lowest local port ID. Ports are numbered in the order the links are listed. On every link the side advertising the better path cost, bridge ID and port ID becomes the designated port and keeps forwarding; a port that is neither root nor designated is an alternate and is blocked, which is what removes the loop, and a topology with N switches and L links leaves L - (N - 1) ports blocked once it has converged. Path costs use the IEEE 802.1t rule of thumb 20,000,000 divided by the link speed in Mb/s, which reproduces the standard values of 2,000,000 at 10 Mb/s, 200,000 at 100 Mb/s, 20,000 at 1 Gb/s, 2,000 at 10 Gb/s and 200 at 100 Gb/s, with any speed from 10 to 1,000,000 Mb/s accepted and rounded. The model assumes point-to-point links, at most one link per pair of switches, equal port priorities and a single common spanning tree (STP, RSTP or the CIST of MSTP), so it does not cover per-VLAN trees, shared media, configured port costs, port roles that only exist while a topology change is in progress, or BPDU filtering. Everything runs locally in your browser and nothing is stored or uploaded.

sources.title: IEEE 802.1D-2004, Media Access Control (MAC) Bridges: root bridge election by lowest bridge ID, root path cost comparison, and the root, designated and alternate port roles.
IEEE 802.1t-2001: recommended path cost values for 10 Mb/s through 10 Gb/s links, reproduced by the 20,000,000 / bandwidth rule of thumb.
IEEE 802.1Q, Bridges and Bridged Networks: the common and internal spanning tree (CIST) that RSTP and MSTP share across a bridged domain.
Cisco, Understanding Spanning Tree Protocol: bridge ID format of priority plus MAC address, default priority 32768 in steps of 4096, and the effect of a lower priority.
